label: Place
name: The Bahamas
summary:
The Bahamas, officially the Commonwealth of the Bahamas, is an island country in the Lucayan Archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean. Comprising more than 3,000 islands, cays, and islets north of Cuba, the Bahamas is home to 400,000 people and is one of the most prosperous nations in the Caribbean, dependent on tourism and offshore financial services.

The Bahamian archipelago was the site of Columbus's first landfall in the Americas on October 12, 1492 — the island he named San Salvador, known to its Lucayan Taíno inhabitants as Guanahani. Within 25 years of contact, the entire Lucayan population (estimated at 30,000–40,000) had been exterminated or enslaved for forced labor in Hispaniola's mines. The islands were subsequently depopulated and ignored by Spain for over a century.

British colonization began in 1648 when a group of Puritan settlers from Bermuda established a colony on Eleuthera. Nassau was founded in 1666. The Bahamas became a notorious pirate haven in the early 18th century — home to Blackbeard, Anne Bonny, and Charles Vane — before Governor Woodes Rogers suppressed piracy (1718). Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution brought enslaved Africans and cotton plantations in the 1780s; emancipation in 1834 transformed the economy. Independence from Britain came in 1973. Today the Bahamas hosts the world's third-largest flag registry and a major offshore banking sector.
